'''''Artemisia filifolia''''',  known by [[common name]]s including '''sand sagebrush''', '''sand sage'''  and '''sandhill sage''', is a [[species]] of flowering plant in the [[Asteraceae|aster family]].<ref name=i>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=250066145 Flora of North America Vol. 19, 20 and 21 Page 508 Sand sage ''Artemisia filifolia'' Torrey, Ann. Lyceum Nat. Hist. New York. 2: 211. 1827. ]</ref> It is native to [[North America]], where it occurs  from [[Nevada]] east to [[South Dakota]] and from there south to [[Arizona]], [[Chihuahua (state)|Chihuahua]], and [[Texas]].<ref name=feis>McWilliams, Jack (2003). [http://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/shrub/artfil/all.html ''Artemisia filifolia''.] In: Fire Effects Information System, [Online]. U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Rocky Mountain Research Station, Fire Sciences Laboratory. Retrieved 12-26-2011.</ref><ref>[http://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Artemisia%20filifolia.png Biota of North America Program 2014 county distribution map]</ref><ref>Turner, B. L. 1996. The Comps of Mexico: A systematic account of the family Asteraceae, vol. 6. Tageteae and Athemideae. Phytologia Memoirs 10: i–ii, 1–22, 43–93.</ref>

==Description==
''Artemisia filifolia''  is a branching woody [[shrub]] growing up to {{convert|1.5|m}} tall. The stems are covered narrow, threadlike leaves up to {{convert|8|cm}} long and no more than half a millimeter wide. The leaves are sometimes split into segments. They are solitary or arranged in [[fascicle (botany)|fascicle]]s. The [[inflorescence]] is a [[panicle]] of hanging [[Head (botany)|flower heads]]. Each head contains sterile disc florets and 2 to 3 fertile ray florets. The fruit is a tiny [[achene]]. The achenes do not tend to [[seed dispersal|disperse]] far from the parent plant.<ref name=feis/><ref name=i/> The leaf color is grayish-green. The flower color is either yellow or brown. The bloom time is between the months of August, September, October, and November.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center - The University of Texas at Austin |url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=ARFI2 |access-date=2023-09-06 |website=www.wildflower.org}}</ref>

==Ecology==
''Artemisia filifolia'' is a [[dominance (ecology)|dominant species]] across much of the west-central United States, particularly in areas where the substrate is a deep, sandy soil.<ref name=feis/> It is an [[indicator species|indicator]] of sandy soils. It is efficient for preventing erosion on such soils.<ref name=utah>[http://extension.usu.edu/range/Woody/sandsage.htm Sand Sagebrush.] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130323041130/http://extension.usu.edu/range/Woody/sandsage.htm |date=March 23, 2013 }} Range Plants of Utah. Utah State University. Retrieved 12-26-2011.</ref> It is common in parts of the [[Great Plains]], where it is a dominant component of [[prairie]], [[grassland]], and [[shrubland]] ecosystems alongside [[grass]]es such as [[andropogon hallii|sand bluestem]], [[bouteloua|grama grasses]], [[Calamovilfa longifolia|sand reedgrass]], [[Schizachyrium scoparium|little bluestem]], and [[sporobolus cryptandrus|sand dropseed]].<ref name=colo>[http://www.cnhp.colostate.edu/download/projects/eco_systems/pdf/WGP_Sandhill_Shrubland.pdf Western Great Plains Sandhill Shrubland.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120426071224/http://www.cnhp.colostate.edu/download/projects/eco_systems/pdf/WGP_Sandhill_Shrubland.pdf |date=2012-04-26 }} Ecosystems. Colorado State. Retrieved 12-26-2011.</ref> Some regions dominated by this sagebrush include the occurrences of the sandsage prairie from Nebraska to central [[Texas]], various river systems in eastern [[Colorado]] and [[Kansas]],<ref name=colo/> the [[sandhill]]s and mixed-grass prairies of Colorado, and parts of southeastern [[Wyoming]]. In Texas, it is common in the [[Trans-Pecos]] region, where it grows with [[Prosopis glandulosa|honey mesquite]], and many other areas in the state where it grows with [[Quercus havardii|sand shinnery oak]].<ref name=feis/>

This ecosystem is most commonly affected by [[wildfire|fire]] and [[grazing]].<ref name=colo/> Before modern fire suppression, the ecosystem was maintained by a pattern of disturbance caused by natural wildfire and grazing by [[bison]], a pattern which is called ''[[Fire ecology|pyric herbivory]]''.

==Rangeland impact==
When humans began to use this terrain as [[rangeland]], this system was altered, causing a [[Species homogeneity|homogenization]] of life forms in the habitat.<ref name=doxon>Doxon, E. D., et al. (2011). [http://web.utk.edu/~edoxon/papers/Doxon%20et%20al%202011b.pdf Aboveground macroinvertebrate diversity and abundance in sand sagebrush prairie managed with the use of pyric herbivory.]{{dead link|date=October 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} ''Rangeland Ecol Manage.'' '''64''' 394-403. Retrieved 12-26-2011.</ref> A balanced regime of fire and grazing is required to sustain the [[biodiversity]] of this type of rangeland.<ref name=winter>Winter, S. L., et al. (2011). [http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1365-2664.2011.02067.x/abstract Restoration of the fire–grazing interaction in ''Artemisia filifolia'' shrubland.] ''Journal of Applied Ecology.'' Online preview. Retrieved 12-26-2011.</ref> Fire also helps prevent the succession of woody vegetation onto shrublands. The sagebrush is tolerant of fire, resprouting vigorously after its aboveground parts are burned away.<ref name=feis/><ref name=vermeire>Vermeire, L. T., et al. [http://www.fs.fed.us/rm/pubs/rmrs_p021/rmrs_p021_233_235.pdf Sand sagebrush response to fall and spring prescribed burning.] In: McArthur, E. Durant, et al. comps. (2001). Shrubland ecosystem genetics and biodiversity: proceedings; 2000 June 13–15; Provo, UT. Proc. RMRS-P-21. Ogden, UT: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Rocky Mountain Research Station. Retrieved 12-26-2011.</ref>

==Ecosystem==
Sand sagebrush ecosystems are important habitat types for many animals. [[Prairie dog]]s build towns in sandy sage grassland, and when they abandon them, [[burrowing owl]]s move in. [[Sage grouse]] live in sand sagebrush, though they prefer [[Artemisia tridentata|big sagebrush]]. Some animals eat the seeds, such as [[lesser prairie chicken]]s and [[scaled quail]].<ref name=feis/> Lesser prairie chickens also use it for cover and nesting purposes.<ref name=vermeire/> Extensive removal of sand sagebrush has been shown to reduce the diversity and abundance of breeding birds in the habitat.<ref name=rod>Rodgers, R. D. and M. L. Sexson. (1990). [http://www.jswconline.org/content/45/4/494.abstract Impacts of extensive chemical control of sand sagebrush on breeding birds.] ''Journal of Soil and Water Conservation.'' '''45'''(4) 494-97. Retrieved 12-26-2011.</ref>

Despite its importance in numerous ecosystems, this sagebrush can become a troublesome [[noxious weed|weed]].<ref name=wilson>Wilson, R. G. (1989). [https://www.jstor.org/pss/3986934 Sand sagebrush (''Artemisia filifolia'') and brittle pricklypear (''Opuntia fragilis'') control.] ''Weed Technology'' '''3'''(2) 272-74. Retrieved 12-26-2011.</ref> One method of control is burning, then placing livestock where they will graze the new sprouts as they come up.<ref name=feis/> It is also controlled with [[herbicide]]s<ref name=wilson/> and [[mowing]].<ref name=feis/>

==Commercial use==
Sand sagebrush seed is sold commercially. It is sometimes used for [[revegetation]] efforts on [[rangeland]] and [[coalfields]].<ref name=feis/> The [[Navajo people|Navajo]] had several uses for the plant. It was used medicinally and for ritual purposes. Being quite soft, it was used as [[toilet paper]].<ref name=feis/><ref name=ethno>[http://extension.usu.edu/range/Woody/sandsage.htm ''Artemisia filifolia''.] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130323041130/http://extension.usu.edu/range/Woody/sandsage.htm |date=March 23, 2013 }} University of Michigan Ethnobotany. Retrieved 12-26-2011.</ref>
